Revision of Proof
Quantification
For all (\forall)
A universal statement claims that a property holds for all members of a given set. Such a statement can be written using the quantifier ‘for all’. For example:

For all real numbers x and y, x^2+5y^2 \geqslant 2xy  or  \forall x,y \in \mathbb{R} ~ (x^2+5y^2 \geqslant 2xy)

To prove this a general argument that applies for all choices of x and y is required.
There exists (\exists)
An existence statement claims that a property holds for at least one member of a given set. Such a statement can be written using the quantifier ‘there exists’. For example:

There exists a triple of integers a,b,c such that a^2+b^2=c^2  or  \exists a,b,c\in \mathbb{Z}~(a^2+b^2=c^2)

To prove that this statement is true, we just need to give one instance.

Negation of Quantifiers
When negating a statement with a quantifier, the quantifiers must also change.

‘There exists’ becomes ‘For all’
‘For all’ becomes ‘There exists’

Example 1.1
Write down the negation of each of the following statements:
(a) For all natural numbers n, we have 2n\geqslant n+1
(b) There exists an integer m such that m^2=4 and m^3= 8
(c) For all real numbers x and y, if x<y, then x^2< y^2
hint: \neg (P \implies Q) = P \land \neg Q


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Disproving Statements
To disprove:

a universal statement, a single counterexample is required
an existence statement, a proof of the negation is required (which is a universal statement)

Example 1.2
Disprove the following:
(a) For all real numbers n, n^2 is either a multiple of 2 or 3.
(b) There exists a natural number n such that n^2+3n+2 is odd.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Divisibility
Example 1.3
Let n\in \mathbb{Z}, prove that n^3-n is divisible by 3.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Conditional Statements
P \implies Q (P implies Q)
P is the hypothesis, Q is the conclusion. Assume P to be true in order to prove.
Example 1.4
Prove that if n is odd, n^2-1 is divisible by 4.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Contrapositive
Remember the contrapositive statement is true if the statement is true.
The contrapositive of P\implies Q is \neg Q \implies \neg P.
Example 1.5
Let n\in \mathbb{Z}, prove that if n^2+2n is odd, then n is odd.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Contradiction
The basic outline of a proof by contradiction is:

Assume that the statement we want to prove is false.
Show that this assumption leads to mathematical nonsense.
Conclude that we were wrong to assume that the statement is false.
Conclude that the statement must be true

Example 1.6
Suppose x satisfies 2^x=5, prove, by contradiction, that x is irrational.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Equivalent Statements
P \iff Q
It can also be said that P is true if and only if Q is true.
This statement states P \implies Q and Q \implies P. To prove an equivalence, both statements must be proven.
Example 1.7
Let n\in\mathbb{Z}, prove that n is divisible by 3 if and only if n^2 is divisible by 3.


                  
                  Solution

Induction
Mathematical Induction is the process of proving a statement by showing it is true for the base case, then showing that if it is true for some integer k, then it is true for k+1; it then follows it must be true for all integers greater than the base case.
The steps are:

Show it is true for the base case, usually (but not always) n=1.
Assume there exists some integer k, where the statement holds.
Show that the statement holds for k+1
Conclude that the statement is true for all integers, greater or equal to the base case, usually (but not always) n\in\mathbb{N}


Partial Sums
Example 3.1
Prove the following for n\in\mathbb{N}, using mathematical induction:
\dfrac{1}{1\times2}+\dfrac{1}{2\times3}+\dfrac{1}{3\times 4}+\dots +\dfrac{1}{n(n+1)}=\dfrac{n}{n+1}

\sum_{i=1}^{n}(2i-1)^3=n^2(2n^2-1)

We have seen previously that infinite or partial sums can be written using sigma notation, \Sigma.
In a similar way, products can be written using pi notation, \Pi.

Position Vectors and Unit Vectors
A vector is defined as having a magnitude (size) and a direction. Vectors are used to represent quantities such as position, velocity, acceleration and forces.

Representing Vectors
The vector \vec{AB} is a line of magnitude |\vec{AB}| and direction starting at A and finishing at B.
A vector can also be expressed with:

The tilde symbol, e.g. \underset{\sim}{a}
Bold notation, e.g. a
Column matrix notation, e.g. \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}
Component form, e.g. x\underset{\sim}{i} + y\underset{\sim}{j} + z\underset{\sim}{k}


Position Vectors and Unit Vectors
Vectors can be written with reference to a certain point, usually the origin, O.

\underset{\sim}{i} is the unit vector in the x direction.
\underset{\sim}{j} is the unit vector in the y direction.
\underset{\sim}{k} is the unit vector in the z direction.


The position vector x\underset{\sim}{i} + y\underset{\sim}{j} + z\underset{\sim}{k} can also be written as \begin{bmatrix} x \\ y \\ z \end{bmatrix}.

Adding and Subtracting Vectors
We add vectors by placing them ‘head to tail’.
In this diagram, \vec{AB} + \vec{BC} = \vec{AC}.

We subtract vectors by reversing the direction of the vector that is subtracted.
\vec{AB} - \vec{BC} = \vec{AB} + \vec{CB}

Scalar Multiplication
Multiplication by a real number (scalar) changes the magnitude, but not the direction, of the vector.
Consider the vector \underset{\sim}{u} = \underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{j}.

2\underset{\sim}{u} is twice the length of \underset{\sim}{u}
\frac{1}{2}\underset{\sim}{u} is half the length of \underset{\sim}{u}
-2\underset{\sim}{u} has double the length, but in the opposite direction


Magnitude of a Vector
The magnitude (or length) of a vector \underset{\sim}{a} = x\underset{\sim}{i} + y\underset{\sim}{j} + z\underset{\sim}{k} is:
|\underset{\sim}{a}| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2 + z^2}

\hat{a} = \frac{\underset{\sim}{a}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}|}

Resolving Vectors
The process of writing a vector as a linear combination of vectors in particular directions is called resolution.
Orthogonal components are at right angles to each other. To represent a vector in space, we resolve the vector along the three mutually perpendicular axes.

Component Form

Scalar (Dot) Product and Projections
The operation of multiplying two vectors has two methods. The dot product (or scalar product) produces a scalar result.

The Dot Product
If \underset{\sim}{a} = a_1\underset{\sim}{i} + a_2\underset{\sim}{j} + a_3\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = b_1\underset{\sim}{i} + b_2\underset{\sim}{j} + b_3\underset{\sim}{k}, the scalar product is:
\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = a_1b_1 + a_2b_2 + a_3b_3

Geometric Interpretation
The scalar product can also be expressed as:
\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = |\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|\cos(\theta)
where \theta is the angle between the two ‘outgoing’ vectors.


Properties of the Scalar Product

The scalar product is a real number, not a vector.
The scalar product is commutative: \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = \underset{\sim}{b} \cdot \underset{\sim}{a}
The scalar product is distributive: \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot (\underset{\sim}{b} + \underset{\sim}{c}) = \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} + \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{c}
m(\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b}) = (m\underset{\sim}{a}) \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot (m\underset{\sim}{b}) for all m \in \mathbb{R}
\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{a} = |\underset{\sim}{a}|^2
The scalar product of perpendicular vectors is 0.


Example 3.1
Find the scalar product of the vectors \underset{\sim}{a} = \underset{\sim}{i} - 2\underset{\sim}{j} + 7\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = 3\underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{k}.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Example 3.2
Find the value of m if the vectors \underset{\sim}{a} = \underset{\sim}{i} - 2\underset{\sim}{j} + 7\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = 3\underset{\sim}{i} + m\underset{\sim}{j} + \underset{\sim}{k} are perpendicular.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Angle Between Two Vectors
To find the angle between two vectors, rearrange the formula:
\cos(\theta) = \frac{\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|}

Example 3.3
Find the angle between the vectors \underset{\sim}{a} = \underset{\sim}{i} - 2\underset{\sim}{j} + 7\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = 3\underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{k}, expressed in degrees correct to two decimal places.

Scalar and Vector Projections
Any vector \underset{\sim}{a} can be written as the sum of two vectors: one parallel to a given vector \underset{\sim}{b} and one perpendicular to \underset{\sim}{b}.

The scalar projection (or scalar resolute) of \underset{\sim}{a} on \underset{\sim}{b} is:
\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \hat{b}
The vector projection (or vector resolute) of \underset{\sim}{a} on \underset{\sim}{b} is (see blue annotations above):
\begin{align}&(\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \hat{b})\hat{b}\\ = &\frac{\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b}}{|\underset{\sim}{b}|^2}\underset{\sim}{b} \\= & \frac{\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b}}{\underset{\sim}{b} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b}}\underset{\sim}{b}\end{align}
The vector projection of \underset{\sim}{a} perpendicular to \underset{\sim}{b} is (see red annotations above):
\underset{\sim}{a} - (\underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \hat{b})\hat{b}

Vector (Cross) Product
The vector product (or cross product) of two vectors in 3D space produces a vector result.
The vector product of two vectors is a vector at right angles to both the original vectors. Its magnitude is the product of the magnitudes of the original vectors and the sine of the angle between their directions. This property makes the cross product essential for finding normals to planes.

The Vector Product Formula
If \underset{\sim}{a} = a_1\underset{\sim}{i} + a_2\underset{\sim}{j} + a_3\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = b_1\underset{\sim}{i} + b_2\underset{\sim}{j} + b_3\underset{\sim}{k}, then:
\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b} = (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)\underset{\sim}{i} - (a_1b_3 - a_3b_1)\underset{\sim}{j} + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)\underset{\sim}{k}

Determinant Form
The vector product can be expressed using determinants:
\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \underset{\sim}{i} & \underset{\sim}{j} & \underset{\sim}{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix} = \begin{vmatrix} a_2 & a_3 \\ b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}\underset{\sim}{i} - \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}\underset{\sim}{j} + \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 \\ b_1 & b_2 \end{vmatrix}\underset{\sim}{k}
where \begin{vmatrix} a & b \\ c & d \end{vmatrix} = ad - bc.

Example 4.1
Find the vector product of the vectors \underset{\sim}{a} = 3\underset{\sim}{i} + 2\underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = \underset{\sim}{i} + 2\underset{\sim}{k}.

Example 4.2
Find the vector product of \underset{\sim}{a} = \begin{bmatrix} 3 \\ -3 \\ 1 \end{bmatrix} and \underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{bmatrix} 4 \\ 9 \\ 2 \end{bmatrix}.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Properties of the Vector Product

\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b} = -(\underset{\sim}{b} \times \underset{\sim}{a}) (anti-commutative)
\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{a} = \underset{\sim}{0} (a vector crossed with itself is the zero vector)
\underset{\sim}{i} \times \underset{\sim}{j} = \underset{\sim}{k}, \underset{\sim}{j} \times \underset{\sim}{k} = \underset{\sim}{i}, \underset{\sim}{k} \times \underset{\sim}{i} = \underset{\sim}{j}


Magnitude of the Cross Product
The magnitude of the vector product is:
|\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b}| = |\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|\sin(\theta)
where \theta is the angle between the two vectors.
The magnitude of the cross product equals the area of the parallelogram formed by vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b}.

Parallel and Perpendicular Vectors
Three important results come from the scalar product:

Key Results

If \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = 0, then vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b} are perpendicular.
If \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = |\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|, then vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b} are parallel in the same direction.
If \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{b} = -|\underset{\sim}{a}||\underset{\sim}{b}|, then vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b} are parallel in the opposite direction.


Collinear Points
If three or more points lie on the same line, they are said to be collinear.
Points A, B, and C are collinear if \vec{AB} is parallel to \vec{AC}, i.e. \vec{AB} = k\vec{AC} for some scalar k.

Concurrent Vectors
If two or more vectors go through the same point, those vectors are said to be concurrent.

Linear Dependence of Vectors

Linear Dependence
If vector \underset{\sim}{c} can be written as a linear combination of vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b}, then \underset{\sim}{a}, \underset{\sim}{b} and \underset{\sim}{c} are said to be linearly dependent.
This means that when \underset{\sim}{c} = m\underset{\sim}{a} + n\underset{\sim}{b} for real numbers m and n, where m and n are not both zero, then \underset{\sim}{a}, \underset{\sim}{b} and \underset{\sim}{c} are linearly dependent.
Also this means that p\underset{\sim}{a}+q\underset{\sim}{b}+r\underset{\sim}{c}=\underset{\sim}{0}, \quad {p,q,r}\in\mathbb{R}

Linear Independence
Conversely, if vector \underset{\sim}{c} cannot be written as a linear combination of vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b}, then \underset{\sim}{a}, \underset{\sim}{b} and \underset{\sim}{c} are said to be linearly independent.
A set of vectors is linearly independent if no vector can be expressed as a linear combination of the other vectors.

Special Case: Two Vectors
For two vectors, they are linearly dependent if and only if they are parallel.
\underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b} are linearly dependent iff \underset{\sim}{a} = m\underset{\sim}{b}, where m is a scalar.

Derivatives of Inverse Functions
The chain rule can be rearranged to show that:
\frac{dy}{dx} = \left(\frac{dx}{dy}\right)^{-1}
This result is useful when a curve is expressed in the form x = f(y), as it allows us to find \frac{dy}{dx} by first finding \frac{dx}{dy} and then taking the reciprocal.

Example 3.1

Example 3.2
A curve has equation x = 1 - y^2. Find \dfrac{dy}{dx} at x = -3.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Derivative of arcsin
Let y = \arcsin(x), then x = \sin(y).
Using the reciprocal relationship and the Pythagorean identity:
\frac{dx}{dy} = \cos(y)
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{\cos(y)} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-\sin^2(y)}} = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
Hence:
\frac{d}{dx}(\arcsin(x)) = \frac{1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}

Derivative of arccos
Let y = \arccos(x), then x = \cos(y).
\frac{dx}{dy} = -\sin(y)
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{-1}{\sin(y)} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-\cos^2(y)}} = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}
Hence:
\frac{d}{dx}(\arccos(x)) = \frac{-1}{\sqrt{1-x^2}}

Derivative of arctan
Let y = \arctan(x), then x = \tan(y).
\frac{dx}{dy} = \sec^2(y) = 1 + \tan^2(y)
\frac{dy}{dx} = \frac{1}{1+\tan^2(y)} = \frac{1}{1+x^2}
Hence:
\frac{d}{dx}(\arctan(x)) = \frac{1}{1+x^2}

Points of Inflection
So far we have seen:

If \frac{dy}{dx} = 0, the function has a stationary point.
If \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} < 0, then it is a local maximum (concave down)
If \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} > 0, then it is a local minimum (concave up)

However, if \frac{d^2y}{dx^2} = 0 the situation is unclear. It could be:

A local maximum
A local minimum
A point of inflection


Types of Points of Inflection
Points of inflection are of two kinds:

A stationary point of inflection (such as y = x^3), when \frac{dy}{dx} = 0
Point of inflection, where the concavity changes (or local point of maximum absolute gradient)

A point of inflection occurs where the sign of the second derivative changes, and so needs to be tested. (see y = \pm x^4)

Cartesian Form
The Imaginary Number i
The number i is defined by the rule i^2 = -1. Practically, this means i = \sqrt{-1}.

Complex Numbers
When a real number is added to an imaginary number, the result is a complex number. All complex numbers have the form z = x + yi where x and y are both real numbers.

x is known as the real part
y is known as the imaginary part

The real part and the imaginary part of a complex number are both real numbers. All real numbers are complex numbers with \text{Im}(z) = 0 and all imaginary numbers are complex numbers with \text{Re}(z) = 0.

Example 1.1
Given that z_1 = 3 - i and z_2 = 2 + 4i
Find:
(a) \text{Re}(z_1)
(b) z_1 + z_2
(c) \text{Im}(z_1 - z_2)
(d) 3z_2 - 2z_1


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





The Argand Diagram
An Argand diagram is a geometric representation of the set of complex numbers. A complex number has two dimensions: the real part and the imaginary part.
Example 1.2
Plot the following complex numbers on the Argand diagram:
(a) 1 + 2i
(b) -1 + 3i
(c) -2 - i
(d) 2 - 3i



                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





When plotted in Cartesian form, we can analogise Complex Numbers with position vectors of points. The operations of vectors then apply to Complex Numbers: e.g. adding complex numbers is the same as “adding vectors tip-to-tail”.
However, there are a couple of specific transformations worth noting:

Multiplication by i
Example 1.3
Plot the following complex numbers on the Argand diagram:
(a) 2 + 3i
(b) (2 + 3i)i
(c) (2 + 3i)i^2
(d) (2 + 3i)i^3
(e) (2 + 3i)i^4



                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Reflection in the x-axis
Example 1.4
Plot the following complex numbers on the Argand diagram:
(a) 2 + 3i
(b) 2 - 3i
(c) -3 + i
(d) -3 - i



                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Multiplication
The product of two complex numbers is achieved in the same way as a binomial product.
Example 1.5
Given that z_1 = 3 - i and z_2 = 2 + 4i
Find:
(a) z_1 z_2
(b) (z_1)^2


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Complex Conjugates
Consider (2 + 3i) \times (2 - 3i):
2 + 3i and 2 - 3i are said to be complex conjugates. Their product is always a real number.
If z = 2 + 3i then \overline{z} = 2 - 3i.

Addition of Two Squares
x^2 + y^2 = (x - yi)(x + yi) = z \times \overline{z}

Example 1.6
If w = 2 - 3i and z = -1 + 2i, find:
(a) \overline{w + z} and \overline{w} + \overline{z}
(b) \overline{w \cdot z} and \overline{w} \cdot \overline{z}


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Modulus
The modulus of a complex number is given by Pythagoras’ Theorem and represents the magnitude of the complex number, in a similar way to the magnitude of a 2D vector.
|z| = \sqrt{(\text{Re}(z))^2 + (\text{Im}(z))^2}
or,
|x + yi| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}

Example 1.7

(a) |z|
(b) |w|
(c) |wz|
(d) |w| \times |z|


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Division
Division of a complex number is similar to dividing by a fraction (multiplicative inverse) followed by rationalising a denominator (multiply top and bottom by the conjugate of the denominator and simplify).
Example 1.8
Find:
(a) z^{-1} if z = 2 - 5i
(b) \dfrac{2 - i}{3 + 2i}

Polar Form I
Polar Form of a Complex Number
The polar form of a complex number uses the modulus r and argument \theta instead of the real and imaginary parts.
z = r(\cos(\theta) + i\sin(\theta)) = r\text{cis}(\theta)
where:

The modulus r = |z| = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
The argument \theta = \text{Arg}(z) is the angle from the positive real axis
The principal argument is in the interval (-\pi, \pi]


Converting Between Forms
Cartesian to Polar:

r = \sqrt{x^2 + y^2}
\tan(\theta) = \dfrac{y}{x} (check quadrant!)

Polar to Cartesian:

x = r\cos(\theta)
y = r\sin(\theta)


Example 2.1
Express each complex number in polar form:
(a) z = 1 + \sqrt{3}i
(b) z = -2 + 2i
(c) z = -\sqrt{3} - i

Example 2.2

(a) z = 4\text{cis}\left(\dfrac{\pi}{3}\right)
(b) z = 2\text{cis}\left(-\dfrac{3\pi}{4}\right)

Multiplication and Division in Polar Form
When multiplying complex numbers in polar form, we multiply the moduli and add the arguments:
r_1\text{cis}(\theta_1) \times r_2\text{cis}(\theta_2) = r_1 r_2 \text{cis}(\theta_1 + \theta_2)
When dividing, we divide the moduli and subtract the arguments:
\frac{r_1\text{cis}(\theta_1)}{r_2\text{cis}(\theta_2)} = \frac{r_1}{r_2}\text{cis}(\theta_1 - \theta_2)

Example 2.3

Distance Between Complex Numbers
The distance between two complex numbers z_1 and z_2 is given by:

Circles in the Complex Plane
The equation |z - z_0| = r represents a circle with centre z_0 and radius r.

|z - z_0| < r is the region inside the circle
|z - z_0| > r is the region outside the circle

Roots of Unity
The nth Roots of Unity
The solutions to z^n = 1 are called the nth roots of unity.
Using De Moivre’s theorem:
z = \text{cis}\left(\frac{2k\pi}{n}\right) \quad \text{for } k = 0, 1, 2, \ldots, n-1
The nth roots of unity are equally spaced around the unit circle, separated by angles of \dfrac{2\pi}{n}.

General Complex Roots
To find the nth roots of a complex number w = r\text{cis}(\theta):

The roots have the same modulus r^{\frac{1}{n}} and are equally spaced around a circle.

Factorising Polynomials
The Fundamental Theorem of Algebra
Every polynomial equation of degree n has exactly n roots (counting multiplicity) over the complex numbers.
This means every polynomial can be factorised into n linear factors over \mathbb{C}.

Factorising Quadratics with Complex Roots
A quadratic az^2 + bz + c = 0 with \Delta = b^2 - 4ac < 0 has complex roots — these are the irreducible quadratic factors encountered in partial fraction decomposition:
z = \frac{-b \pm \sqrt{b^2 - 4ac}}{2a} = \frac{-b \pm i\sqrt{|\Delta|}}{2a}

Example 6.1

The Conjugate Root Theorem
If P(z) is a polynomial with real coefficients and x + yi is a root of P(z) = 0, then x - yi is also a root.

Example 6.2

Factor Theorem: (z - a) is a factor of P(z) if and only if P(a) = 0.

Curves in 2D and 3D
Vector Equations of Curves
A curve in 2D or 3D can be described by a vector equation (also called a parametric vector equation):
\underset{\sim}{r}(t) = x(t)\underset{\sim}{i} + y(t)\underset{\sim}{j} + z(t)\underset{\sim}{k}
where t is the parameter and x(t), y(t), z(t) are functions of t.

x = x(t)
y = y(t)
z = z(t)


Example 1.1
Given the vector equation \underset{\sim}{r}(t) = (2+3t)\underset{\sim}{i} + (1-t)\underset{\sim}{j} + (4+2t)\underset{\sim}{k}, write the parametric equations for the curve.

Vector Equation of a Line
Position Vectors and Displacement Vectors
The position vector of a point A, written \overrightarrow{OA}, is the vector from the origin O to the point A. It is usually written as the lower case vector \underset{\sim}{a}.
The displacement vector from A to B, written \overrightarrow{AB}, is given by:
\overrightarrow{AB} = \underset{\sim}{b} - \underset{\sim}{a}

Vector Equation of a Line
The vector equation of a straight line through point A(a_1, a_2, a_3) with position vector \underset{\sim}{a} in the direction of vector \underset{\sim}{d} is:
\underset{\sim}{r}(t) = \underset{\sim}{a} + t\underset{\sim}{d}, \quad t \in \mathbb{R}
Note: There are infinitely many valid choices for both \underset{\sim}{a} (any point on the line) and \underset{\sim}{d} (any scalar multiple).
For a line through points A and B with position vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b}:
\underset{\sim}{r}(t) = \underset{\sim}{a} + t\overrightarrow{AB} = \underset{\sim}{a} + t(\underset{\sim}{b} - \underset{\sim}{a}), \quad t \in \mathbb{R}

Example 2.1
Find the vector equation of the line through (3, 5, 1) and (-3, 3, 4).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Parametric Form
By expanding the vector equation \underset{\sim}{r}(t) = \underset{\sim}{a} + t\underset{\sim}{d}, we obtain the parametric equations:

x = a_1 + td_1
y = a_2 + td_2
z = a_3 + td_3

where (a_1, a_2, a_3) is a point on the line and \begin{pmatrix} d_1 \\ d_2 \\ d_3 \end{pmatrix} is the direction vector.

Example 2.2
Find the vector equation and parametric form of the line through (3, -4, 4) and (-2, 3, 1).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Cartesian Form
The Cartesian equation of a line in 3D is:
\frac{x - a_1}{d_1} = \frac{y - a_2}{d_2} = \frac{z - a_3}{d_3}
This is derived by making t the subject in each parametric equation and equating.
Note: If any component of \underset{\sim}{d} is zero, that coordinate is constant along the line.

Example 2.3
Find the Cartesian equation of the line through (3, 6, 2) and (-1, -4, 0).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Line Segments
For a line segment from A to B:

If 0 \leqslant t \leqslant 1, the points are on the line segment AB
If t < 0, the points are on the line to the left of A
If t > 1, the points are to the right of B

Normals to a Plane
The cross product (or vector product) of two vectors produces a vector that is perpendicular (normal) to both original vectors. This is essential for finding normals to planes.

Cross Product Formula
For vectors \underset{\sim}{a} = a_1\underset{\sim}{i} + a_2\underset{\sim}{j} + a_3\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = b_1\underset{\sim}{i} + b_2\underset{\sim}{j} + b_3\underset{\sim}{k}:
\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{vmatrix} \underset{\sim}{i} & \underset{\sim}{j} & \underset{\sim}{k} \\ a_1 & a_2 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}
Expanding using cofactors:
\underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b} = \begin{vmatrix} a_2 & a_3 \\ b_2 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}\underset{\sim}{i} - \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_3 \\ b_1 & b_3 \end{vmatrix}\underset{\sim}{j} + \begin{vmatrix} a_1 & a_2 \\ b_1 & b_2 \end{vmatrix}\underset{\sim}{k}
= (a_2b_3 - a_3b_2)\underset{\sim}{i} - (a_1b_3 - a_3b_1)\underset{\sim}{j} + (a_1b_2 - a_2b_1)\underset{\sim}{k}

Example 3.1
If \underset{\sim}{a} = 2\underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = -3\underset{\sim}{i} + 4\underset{\sim}{j} + \underset{\sim}{k}, calculate:
(a) \underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b}
(b) \underset{\sim}{b} \times \underset{\sim}{a}


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Finding a Normal to a Plane
A plane is a flat surface in 3D that extends in all directions. A normal to the plane is a vector perpendicular to the plane.
Given two non-parallel vectors \underset{\sim}{a} and \underset{\sim}{b} that lie in a plane, the cross product \underset{\sim}{a} \times \underset{\sim}{b} gives a vector normal to the plane.

Example 3.2
The plane \Gamma_1 contains position vectors \underset{\sim}{a} = 4\underset{\sim}{i} - 2\underset{\sim}{j} + 2\underset{\sim}{k} and \underset{\sim}{b} = -4\underset{\sim}{i} + 5\underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k}. Find a normal to \Gamma_1 and a unit normal vector.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Normal to a Plane Using Three Points
Any three points A, B and C not in a straight line are sufficient to specify a plane. We can find a normal to a plane by finding the vector product of two displacement vectors: \overrightarrow{AB} \times \overrightarrow{AC}.

Example 3.3
The points A(5, 2, -1), B(6, -6, 5) and C(1, -4, 3) are on the plane \Pi_1.
Find the equation of the plane in the form \underset{\sim}{r}(s,t) = \underset{\sim}{a} + s\underset{\sim}{d_1} + t\underset{\sim}{d_2}, where \underset{\sim}{d_1} and \underset{\sim}{d_2} are two non-parallel vectors that lie in the plane. Also find the normal vector to the plane.

Vector Equations of Planes
Equation of a Plane from a Normal and a Point
A plane can be defined by:

A point A(x_0, y_0, z_0) with position vector \underset{\sim}{a}
A normal vector \underset{\sim}{n} perpendicular to the plane

For any point P with position vector \underset{\sim}{r} on the plane, the vector \underset{\sim}{r} - \underset{\sim}{a} lies in the plane and is perpendicular to \underset{\sim}{n}:
(\underset{\sim}{r} - \underset{\sim}{a}) \cdot \underset{\sim}{n} = 0
This can be rearranged to:
\underset{\sim}{r} \cdot \underset{\sim}{n} = \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{n} = k
The Cartesian equation of the plane through A(x_0, y_0, z_0) with normal \underset{\sim}{n} = a\underset{\sim}{i} + b\underset{\sim}{j} + c\underset{\sim}{k} is:
ax + by + cz = k
where k = ax_0 + by_0 + cz_0.

Example 4.1
Find the equation of a plane with normal 2\underset{\sim}{i} + 4\underset{\sim}{j} + 3\underset{\sim}{k} containing the point (3, -2, 7).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Example 4.2
Write the vector equation of a plane with normal -3\underset{\sim}{i} + 2\underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k} containing the point (2, 1, 5).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Equation of a Plane from Three Points
Given three non-collinear points P, Q, R:

Find two vectors in the plane: e.g. \overrightarrow{PQ} and \overrightarrow{PR}
Calculate the normal: \underset{\sim}{n} = \overrightarrow{PQ} \times \overrightarrow{PR}
Use any of the three points to form the equation


Example 4.3
Find the equation of a plane containing the points (1, 2, -7), (3, -5, 6) and (-4, 2, 8).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Checking if a Point Lies on a Plane
To check if a point (x_0, y_0, z_0) lies on a plane with equation ax + by + cz = k:
Substitute the coordinates into the equation and verify equality.

Example 4.4
Determine whether each of the following points is on the plane 2x - 3y + 5z = 7:
(a) (5, -4, -3)
(b) (-8, -1, 5)


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Parallel Planes
Two planes are parallel if their normal vectors are parallel (scalar multiples of each other).
The equation of a plane parallel to ax + by + cz = k_1 has the form:
ax + by + cz = k_2

Example 4.5
Find the equation of the plane that is parallel to 4x - y + 5z = 6 and passes through the point (3, 1, -3).


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Summary
A plane can be defined in 3 ways:


A point and two vectors in the plane: \underset{\sim}{r}(t) = \underset{\sim}{a} + s\underset{\sim}{d_1} + t\underset{\sim}{d_2}


A point and a normal vector: \underset{\sim}{r} \cdot \underset{\sim}{n} = k, where \underset{\sim}{n} = \underset{\sim}{d_1} \times \underset{\sim}{d_2} and k = \underset{\sim}{a} \cdot \underset{\sim}{n}


Cartesian form: n_i x + n_j y + n_k z = k where \underset{\sim}{n} = \begin{pmatrix} n_i \\ n_j \\ n_k \end{pmatrix} is the normal vector.

Distances, Intersections and Angles
Distance from a Point to a Plane
The distance from a point P to a plane \Pi is given by:
D = |\vec{PQ} \cdot \hat{n}|
where \hat{n} is the unit normal to the plane and Q is any point on the plane.

Example 5.1
Find the distance from the point P(1, 4, 3) to the plane \Pi: 2x - 3y + 6z = -1.


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Example 5.2
Find the distance between the parallel planes given by:
\Pi_1: 2x - y + 2z = 5, \quad \Pi_2: 2x - y + 2z = -2


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Intersections and Angles
The angle of intersection of two planes is equal to the angle of the normals to the two planes. The intersection of two planes is a line.

Example 5.3
For planes:
\Pi_1: \underset{\sim}{r} \cdot (\underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{j} - 3\underset{\sim}{k}) = 6, \quad \Pi_2: \underset{\sim}{r} \cdot (2\underset{\sim}{i} - \underset{\sim}{j} + \underset{\sim}{k}) = 4
Find:
(a) the angle between the planes
(b) the vector equation of line of intersection between the planes


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Example 5.4
Consider the line represented by the equation \underset{\sim}{r} = 3\underset{\sim}{i} - \underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k} + t(\underset{\sim}{i} + 2\underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k}) and the plane represented by the equation \underset{\sim}{r} \cdot (\underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{j} + 2\underset{\sim}{k}) = 2.
Find:
(a) the point of intersection
(b) the angle between the line and the plane (which is 90° - \theta to the normal to the plane)


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Distance between Two Parallel Planes
For two parallel planes \Pi_1: ax + by + cz = k_1 and \Pi_2: ax + by + cz = k_2, the distance between them is:
D = \frac{|k_1 - k_2|}{|\underset{\sim}{n}|} = \frac{|k_1 - k_2|}{\sqrt{a^2 + b^2 + c^2}}
Method:

Ensure both plane equations have the same normal vector (same coefficients for x, y, z).
Apply the formula above, or
Pick any point on one plane and find its distance to the other plane using the point-to-plane formula.


Example 5.5
Find the distance between the parallel planes:
\Pi_1: 3x - 2y + 6z = 14 \quad \text{and} \quad \Pi_2: 3x - 2y + 6z = -7


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Distance between Two Skew Lines
The minimum distance between two lines of skew will be perpendicular to both lines.
For two skew lines:
\underset{\sim}{r_1} = \underset{\sim}{a_1} + \lambda\underset{\sim}{d_1}, \quad \underset{\sim}{r_2} = \underset{\sim}{a_2} + \mu\underset{\sim}{d_2}
The distance is given by:
D = |\vec{PQ} \cdot \hat{\underset{\sim}n}|
\Rightarrow D = \left|(\underset{\sim}{a_1} - \underset{\sim}{a_2}) \cdot \left(\frac{\underset{\sim}{d_1} \times \underset{\sim}{d_2}}{|\underset{\sim}{d_1} \times \underset{\sim}{d_2}|}\right)\right|

Example 5.6

\underset{\sim}{r_1} = \underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{j} + \lambda(2\underset{\sim}{i} - \underset{\sim}{j} + \underset{\sim}{k}), \quad \underset{\sim}{r_2} = 2\underset{\sim}{i} + \underset{\sim}{j} - \underset{\sim}{k} + \mu(3\underset{\sim}{i} - 5\underset{\sim}{j} + 2\underset{\sim}{k})

Sketching Anti-Derivative Graphs
Given the graph of y = f(x), we can sketch the graph of an antiderivative y = F(x) by noting:

Where f(x) > 0, F(x) is increasing
Where f(x) < 0, F(x) is decreasing
Where f(x) = 0, F(x) has a stationary point
Where f(x) has a local maximum, F(x) has a point of inflection
Where f(x) has a local minimum, F(x) has a point of inflection

Defining a Function as an Integral
Consider the integral \displaystyle{\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\, dt}
By the fundamental theorem of calculus this is equal to F(x)-F(a), where F is an antiderivative of f.
Therefore:
\dfrac{d}{dx}\bigg(\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\, dt\bigg) = f(x)
This means that if we define a function g(x) = \displaystyle{\int_{a}^{x}f(t)\, dt}, then:

g is decreasing when f(x) < 0

Arc Length
Derivation of Arc Length Formula
To find the length of a curve between points, consider a small segment from (x, y) to (x + \delta x, y + \delta y).
Using Pythagoras’ theorem:
\delta s \approx \sqrt{(\delta x)^2 + (\delta y)^2} = \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{\delta y}{\delta x}\right)^2} \cdot \delta x
As \delta x \to 0:
ds = \sqrt{1 + \left(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\right)^2} \, dx

Length of a Curve
The length of a curve y=f(x) from x=a to x=b is given by:
L=\int_{a}^{b}\sqrt{1+\bigg(\dfrac{dy}{dx}\bigg)^2}\, dx
If the curve is given parametrically as x = x(t) and y = y(t), then:
L=\int_{t_1}^{t_2}\sqrt{\bigg(\dfrac{dx}{dt}\bigg)^2+\bigg(\dfrac{dy}{dt}\bigg)^2}\, dt

Introduction to Differential Equations
A differential equation is an equation that involves a function and its derivative(s). The solution to the equation is the function itself.
The order of a differential equation is its highest derivative and the degree is the highest power of the highest derivative.
For example:

\dfrac{dy}{dx}=5xy is of order 1, degree 1, and y is the function
\dfrac{d^2y}{dx^2}+4\dfrac{dy}{dx}+4=0 is of order 2, degree 1
\left(\dfrac{dP}{ds}\right)^3-\left(\dfrac{d^2P}{ds^2}\right)+P=0 is of order 2, degree 3

Differential equations are used to model many real-life situations including velocity, force, temperature change, and population growth.

Verifying a Solution to a Differential Equation
A solution can be shown to satisfy a differential equation by substituting the solution into the equation. This will involve differentiating the solution before substitution.

Models and Applications
Sometimes differential equations are given in terms of the dependent variable. In this case we need to separate the variables:
\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(y)
\Rightarrow \int\dfrac{1}{f(y)}\,dy=\int 1 \cdot dx
\Rightarrow \int\dfrac{1}{f(y)}\,dy=x+c

Example 4.1
Find a general solution to:
(a) \dfrac{dy}{dx}=4y-3,\quad y>\dfrac{3}{4}
(b) \dfrac{dy}{dx}=e^{2y}
(c) \dfrac{dy}{dx}=1-y^2


                  
                  Solution 
                  
                





Newton’s Law of Cooling
Newton’s law of cooling states that the rate at which an object loses heat is proportional to the temperature difference between the object and its surroundings.
It can be expressed as \dfrac{dT}{dt}=-k(T-T_s), where T is the temperature of the object at time t, T_s is the temperature of the surroundings, and k is a proportionality constant.
The general solution is T=T_s+T_0e^{-kt}, where T_0 is the initial temperature difference.

Example 4.2

Find, to the nearest minute, how long it will take for the temperature of the rod to drop to 40^\circC.

Growth and Decay
Natural elements such as uranium and carbon gradually transform into different substances. The time they take to do this can be modelled mathematically. The rate of decay is proportional to the quantity present: \dfrac{dN}{dt}=-kN for decay, or \dfrac{dN}{dt}=kN for growth.

Example 4.3

After 2 hours it is observed that 20% has disintegrated. Determine the amount remaining after a further 3 hours, correct to 3 decimal places.

\dfrac{dM}{dt}=\text{inflow rate}-\text{outflow rate}

Separation of Variables
A first-order, degree 1, differential equation of the form \dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y) allows the variables to be separated and anti-differentiation to be performed.
\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)g(y)
\dfrac{1}{g(y)}\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}=f(x)
This is called separation of variables because we have the y-terms on the left and the x-terms on the right.
Integrate both sides with respect to x:
\int\dfrac{1}{g(y)}\,\dfrac{dy}{dx}\,dx=\int f(x)\,dx
\int\dfrac{1}{g(y)}\,dy=\int f(x)\,dx

Euler’s Method
Euler’s method is a numerical method for finding solutions to differential equations that cannot be solved algebraically. Numerical methods like this are generally used to solve all real world differential equations as algebraic solutions are usually unavailable.
Euler’s Method

This is an approximation as it assumes a linear change in the interval [x_n,x_n+h]. The approximation is better for smaller h, at the cost of compute time.

Key Concepts

Linear combinations: E(aX + b) = aE(X) + b, \text{Var}(aX + b) = a^2\text{Var}(X)
Normal distribution: X \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2)
Standard normal: Z \sim N(0, 1)
z-score: Z = \frac{X - \mu}{\sigma}
Sampling distribution: \bar{X} \sim N(\mu, \sigma^2/n)
Central Limit Theorem
Confidence intervals: \bar{x} \pm z \cdot \frac{\sigma}{\sqrt{n}}
Hypothesis testing: H_0, H_1, p-value, significance level
Type I error (\alpha) and Type II error (\beta)
Power of a test: 1 - \beta
